claims.claim: IREN's core structural bridge is power/data-center infrastructure to scarce accelerated-compute capacity serving hyperscaler AI demand; the Microsoft agreement supplies customer-linked evidence for that bridge.
Once demand is contracted, the successor bottleneck moves to financing, power delivery, construction, GPU procurement, commissioning and operating reliability.

factors.name: bottleneckControl
factors.basis: Power and data-center footprint can control a scarce physical input to AI compute deployment.

factors.name: scenarioRobustness
factors.basis: Contracted hyperscaler demand supports utilization, but concentrated customer exposure and phased execution create binary schedule risk.

factors.name: substitutionResilience
factors.basis: Compute demand is robust, but hyperscalers can self-build or source from competing infrastructure providers.

causalEdges.mechanism: larger training and inference workloads require GPU compute, power and data-center capacity
causalEdges.falsifier: compute-efficiency gains or demand slowdown materially reduce required external capacity

causalEdges.mechanism: energized sites and physical infrastructure allow large GPU clusters to be installed and operated
causalEdges.falsifier: power, construction, networking, cooling or GPU constraints prevent commissioning

causalEdges.mechanism: commissioned contracted capacity converts infrastructure into customer service revenue
causalEdges.falsifier: phases slip materially, contract terms change, or delivered economics fail to support expected returns

risks.risk: Successor bottlenecks are capital and execution intensive and can delay conversion of contracted demand into operating capacity.
Customer concentration reduces resilience if a major contract is modified or not renewed.

unknowns.unknown: Current phase-by-phase commissioning status and realized economics are not established by the reused source.

claims.claim: The $9.7 billion headline contract and expected run-rate revenue are not equivalent to recognized revenue, cash flow or return on capital; delivery requires a roughly $5.8 billion Dell equipment purchase and phased commissioning.

factors.name: financingRisk
factors.basis: Large equipment and infrastructure commitments create substantial capital requirements before full revenue conversion.

factors.name: concentrationRisk
factors.basis: A very large named customer contract can make execution and renewal outcomes disproportionately important.

factors.name: confidenceInflation
factors.basis: Contract value and annualized run-rate should not be treated as present revenue or profit before commissioning.

risks.risk: Construction, energization, GPU delivery and commissioning slippage can defer revenue while capital obligations remain.
Hyperscaler self-build and competing GPU-cloud providers can pressure renewal economics over time.
The evidence base is currently concentrated in one issuer source and lacks a fresher phase-by-phase commissioning update.

contradictions.claim: Large contracted demand versus still-unproven realized phase economics.
contradictions.resolution: Contract validates demand but not completion, margin or return; preserve both facts without treating the latter uncertainty as a present contradiction blocker.

unknowns.unknown: Financing mix, realized margins and current delivery status for all phases remain unknown in this lineage.
